messages.subject: Potential second edition of SFLWR: wishlist
messages.subject_clean: Potential second edition of SFLWR: wishlist
messages.body_plain:
Hi all

Mouton has contacted me to ask whether I would be interested in
working on a revised and extended edition of the stats textbook (it
seems to sell well) and whether I would have ideas about what, apart
from fixing errors, I would want to change/add. I gave this some
thought and I do in fact have quite a variety of ideas but I also
thought, why not ask you for what *you* think could be nice so here's
your chance: if you have any ideas on what you would like to see in
there, respond to this thread. I, and probably readers of a such a
second edition, would be grateful for any input you may have. Of
course, I cannot promise that I can incorporate whatever suggestions
you may have - if there are any to begin with, that is - but I am
definitely open for your ideas so let me know what you think ...

Cheers,
STG
--
Stefan Th. Gries
-----------------------------------------------
University of California, Santa Barbara
http://www.linguistics.ucsb.edu/faculty/stgries
-----------------------------------------------

messages.body_plain:
Hi Stefan,

I think this is a great opportunity for you to address mixed-effects
modeling.  I've always preferred your text over other similar stats for
linguists books for it's clarity. I'd love to read your take on
mixed-effects.

Best,
-Derek Denis
Department of Linguistics
University of Toronto

messages.body_plain:
Hi Stefan,

In addition to mixed-effects models requests, which I suppose are
going to be on high demand. I wonder if you would consider including
approaches such as classifier/decision trees such as Random Forest
(ala Leo Breiman). At least people should be aware of these
approaches, I believe. My five cents.

Best wishes,

Heriberto

messages.body_plain:
yes, Stefan, random forests would be really nice. and more generally, I would love to learn more about some of the other classifiers available in R, e.g. adaptive boost models (ada) , support vector machines (ksvm) and maybe even single hidden layer neural networks (nnet). all of these tend to outperform glms in my data (and seem to have additional advantages as well).

cheers,
daniel

messages.body_plain:
I too would like to see how you present and discuss mixed-effects
models (possibly/probably with Bates' lme4 package ?). I also enjoy
your clarity and especially the suggestions you give on how to word
the interpretation of results, something I haven't seen much of in
other similar works. It's helpful for newbies to (non-GoldVarb) stats
like me.
